title: Meta Ran Ads for an App That Promised to Nudify Female Politicians
gist: Meta ran ads for Kromix, an AI 'nudify' tool that promoted creating deepfake porn of female US politicians, despite policies banning such content—the latest failure of its AI-reliant ad-review system after it laid off human moderators. Apple removed Kromix and MaskAI from the App Store after WIRED inquiries, part of a broader regulatory and enforcement pressure on nonconsensual-intimate-imagery apps.

insights.claim: Meta ran ads for the AI porn tool Kromix targeting male users, with one ad showing a woman resembling a prominent female US politician before cutting to a pornographic scene, despite Meta's explicit policies banning sexual imagery and nudify-app promotion.
insights.speaker: Vittoria Elliott
insights.so_what: Repeated policy-enforcement gaps expose Meta to regulatory and reputational liability around its core ad product.

insights.claim: The account behind the campaign ran 32 ads for five-to-46 hours each and was created on August 3 with no followers—signals Meta's automated review could have flagged as suspicious but did not.
insights.speaker: Vittoria Elliott
insights.so_what: New, follower-less pages slipping through review points to a systemic, exploitable weakness in ad onboarding.

insights.claim: Meta removed 344,000 ads promoting nudify services on Facebook and Instagram between November and January and filed a lawsuit against at least one firm, yet researchers keep finding thousands the company failed to detect.
insights.speaker: Vittoria Elliott
insights.so_what: Enforcement volume at scale still leaves a persistent detection gap, undercutting Meta's AI-moderation claims.

insights.claim: Katie Paul of the Tech Transparency Project argues Meta has increasingly relied on AI to vet ads while laying off human moderators, leaving 'zero quality control' on its primary product.
insights.speaker: Katie Paul
insights.so_what: Ties the enforcement failures directly to a cost-cutting shift from human to AI moderation, a structural risk factor.
insights.quote: Ads are Meta’s primary product, and there appears to be zero quality control

insights.claim: Most Kromix video ads used benign cover photos of beaches, mountains, or waterfalls to disguise pornographic content, an adversarial tactic Meta says it is aware of but that still bypassed its systems.
insights.speaker: Cindy Southworth
insights.so_what: Cover-image obfuscation is a repeatable circumvention pattern that automated visual review struggles to catch.
insights.quote: no system is perfect, and we’re continuing to investigate why these ads were able to bypass our systems

insights.claim: Apple removed Kromix and, separately, an app called MaskAI from the App Store after WIRED inquiries, saying Kromix appeared to add prohibited content and features after initial review.
insights.speaker: Vittoria Elliott
insights.so_what: Post-approval feature-swapping is how bad-actor apps evade App Store review, a recurring platform-gatekeeping failure.

insights.claim: San Francisco's city attorney sent Apple a cease-and-desist letter demanding removal of 13 specific nudify apps and that it stop 'aiding and abetting' the sale of explicit deepfake images.
insights.speaker: Vittoria Elliott
insights.so_what: Municipal legal pressure signals rising regulatory exposure for platform gatekeepers over hosted deepfake tools.

insights.claim: Politicians and elected officials—overwhelmingly women—have been targeted by nonconsensual deepfakes for years, with Grok used in January to create around 3 million sexualized images of women and girls, including officials in Sweden, England, and Northern Ireland.
insights.speaker: Vittoria Elliott
insights.so_what: Quantifies how mass, cheap AI image generation industrializes gender-based harassment of public figures.

insights.claim: Benjamin Shultz of the American Sunlight Project says democratized AI generation has turned benign media like official portraits and press-conference video into raw material for no-code tools anyone with internet access can use.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Shultz
insights.so_what: Frames the threat as a structural shift lowering the cost and skill barrier to producing harmful deepfakes.
insights.quote: formerly benign media—official portraits, video from a press conference—have become raw material for low- and no-code tools

insights.claim: Tech Transparency Project researchers found more than 50 ads on Meta's platforms containing AI child sexual abuse material and images of minors with sexually suggestive statements, some of which ran after Meta said it had introduced new AI to better detect violating ads at upload.
insights.speaker: Vittoria Elliott
insights.so_what: CSAM ads slipping through after new AI safeguards is a severe compliance and legal-liability signal for Meta.
